Norman Mailer. He lived from nineteen twenty-three to two thousand seven, an American novelist, essayist, and provocateur whose fiction and nonfiction tackle American power, sexuality, violence, and the masculine ego with unflinching intensity. His work spans war novels and innovative narrative nonfiction. He was celebrated and reviled equally for his uncompromising style and contentious public persona, remaining one of the most influential American writers of the postwar period.

The Naked and the Dead came in nineteen forty-eight as his debut war novel set in the Pacific—a massive bestseller that established him as a major voice immediately. The Armies of the Night, published in nineteen sixty-eight, pioneered a new kind of journalism about the nineteen sixty-seven March on the Pentagon, winning the Pulitzer Prize. Then came Ancient Evenings in nineteen eighty-three, a sprawling metaphysical novel set in ancient Egypt that demonstrates his ambition and formal risk-taking.

He won the Pulitzer Prize twice, in nineteen sixty-nine and nineteen eighty, plus the National Book Award and numerous other recognitions. His essays shaped American cultural criticism; Advertisements for Myself from nineteen fifty-nine collects provocative pieces on literature, power, and art. He wrote about sexuality and violence with unprecedented candor. His testosterone-soaked masculinity was both his subject and his style. He lived publicly and controversially, making his life and work inseparable—the author as protagonist and sage.

He shares this territory with Philip Roth as a Jewish-American novelist equally engaged with American identity and transgression. He drew from Saul Bellow's intellectual depth but channeled it through a more combative register. American excess was central to his vision: America as a nation of amplified desire, power, and violence. He pioneered blending reportage with novelistic technique and authorial presence.
